newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Two bombs rock Tajik capital despite truce deal.
newsitem.headline: Two bombs rock Tajik capital despite truce deal.

text.p: Two bombs rocked the centre of the Tajik capital Dushanbe on Thursday, killing one person and injuring another, hours after a new ceasefire was scheduled to take hold in the former Soviet republic.
"The blasts were caused by two explosive devices," Interior Minister Khumdin Sharipov told Reuters by telephone, adding that he had no information on who planted them.
A corpse lay near Dushanbe's main post office where the first explosion went off shortly after midday (0700 GMT).
Bystanders said an injured person had been taken to hospital after the blast which smashed windows in nearby buildings.
The second bomb near the Pakistan embassy wrecked a Lada car. The buildings were quickly sealed off by police.

Nerves in the Tajik capital are on edge following a spate of attacks against Russian servicemen who help prop up Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov's shaky administration after four years of civil war.
The recent attacks have been widely blamed on opposition guerrillas, but the opposition has not claimed responsibility.
"The opposition had no hand in this," Yusuf Khakimov, an opposition representative based Dushanbe, said after Thursday's explosions. "It is not in our interests."

Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov and Islamic opposition leader Sayid Abdullo Nuri agreed the ceasefire -- which was supposed to come into effect at midnight local time on Wednesday -- during talks in northern Afghanistan earlier this week.
The truce is intended to pave the way for a peace accord, to be signed in Moscow on December 19.
"It could have been the opposition," said a western diplomat based in the capital. "But there are also a lot of hardliners in the government who don't want this peace accord to work."
Many previous ceasefires have been routinely flouted in the remote, mountainous republic of 5.7 million people bordering Afghanistan and China.
A United Nations-sponsored ceasefire reconfirmed in July began to collapse shortly after it was signed.
"We're not exactly glowing with hope about it," the diplomat said of the latest agreement.
The civil war has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced many more in Tajikistan, where regional and clan rivalries underlie the war between the secular government and Islamist guerrillas.
